posts.title: One of the biggest mistakes in crypto investigations is assuming that a line on a tracing chart proves a relationship.
posts.author: JP Intelligence on Chain (IOC)
posts.snippet:
One of the biggest mistakes in crypto investigations is assuming that a line on a tracing chart proves a relationship.

It doesn’t.

A transaction can represent:

→ A genuine transfer between two people
→ Exchange infrastructure
→ A smart contract interaction
→ Address poisoning
→ Zero-value spam
→ Automated routing
→ Something completely unrelated to your hypothesis

The further you investigate, the more dangerous simplistic heuristics become.

Try to disprove your own connections.

That’s an important distinction.
posts.reason: A thoughtful discussion on the pitfalls of simplistic crypto tracing heuristics directly aligns with Bloctopus's forensics expertise and would resonate with lawyers, compliance officers, and law enforcement.

comments.text: This is exactly where forensic reports fall apart under cross-examination - counsel asks whether the analyst tried to disprove their own hypothesis, and if the answer is no, the whole chart's evidentiary weight drops. Address poisoning and zero-value spam are the two we see junior analysts miss most often.
Do you run a formal falsification step before a chart goes into a report, or is disproving the connection something that happens informally as you go?

We've had cases where a single unverified 'link' on a chart nearly became the basis of a legal claim, until we traced the counterparty address back to exchange hot wallet infrastructure. The chart was technically accurate and substantively misleading.

posts.author: Don Prince
posts.snippet:
While NodeAI OS works seamlessly online, it wasn't built for pristine corporate offices with unlimited fiber. It is engineered for the real world—where a weak, metered 4G mobile hotspot is your entire lifeline.
For anyone who remembers the screeching handshake of 90s dial-up, you know the anxiety of a fragile connection. That is the exact reality our software lives in. When users deploy at the edge, they can't casually pull gigabytes of updates, run fragile cloud dependencies, or stall out on remote mirrors.
Because a metered cellular link is our standard working reality, we’ve stripped away all reliance on the external web. Every core subsystem of NodeAI OS is engineered for absolute self-reliance:
Pre-Loaded Intelligence: Heavy AI models, graphics suites, and core tooling are baked directly into encrypted local storage. The system never needs to "call home" to execute local inference.
Zero-Download Boot Sequence: Instead of pulling packages at launch, the OS instantly mounts local, pre-packaged software overlays on boot.
Self-Contained Display Stack: Dynamic hardware detection probes and configures the GPU acceleration pipeline entirely offline—no waiting on remote driver downloads.
Persistent Side-Loading: Built on a battle-tested Linux foundation, NodeAI OS includes broad out-of-the-box hardware support while allowing offline driver side-loading via persistent storage.
Live OS Architecture: Designed for clean, deterministic operations and effortless factory resets, avoiding Secure Boot friction to deliver a true "Plug and Infer" experience.
Adaptive Legacy Hardware Revival: Dynamically reconfigures runtimes to bring older, asymmetric, or heterogeneous hardware setups back into active service.
We didn't design NodeAI OS expecting a perfect connection; we designed it to master a restricted one. By treating low-bandwidth 4G as our native environment, we’ve built an AI operating system that doesn't just survive at the edge—it thrives there completely offline.

posts.title: 10,000 combinations.
posts.author: Iheb Eddine BADRANI
posts.snippet:
10,000 combinations. 

That is all an infostealer malware needs to brute-force a 4-digit PIN once it dumps your browser profile folder.

Yet almost every browser password manager offers a 4-digit PIN for convenience. That PIN usually encrypts your master keys on disk. On modern hardware, 10,000 iterations cracks in seconds.

When building the browser extension for Keygrain—an open-source deterministic credential generator that calculates credentials mathematically rather than storing a vault—we made our first design rule non-negotiable:

Zero low-entropy secrets on disk. No persistent PINs. Ever.

But that immediately triggered a classic product nightmare:
"If you kill the PIN, won't users have to type a 20-character master passphrase 50 times a day just to view their logins?"

If security turns the product into an obstacle course, users will bypass it or uninstall it.

Here is how we solved this using a Two-Tier Ephemeral State Machine in Chrome & Firefox (diagram below):

1. The Background Worker is the Cryptographic Firewall
The popup UI and content scripts are treated as completely untrusted presentation layers. They never touch derivation keys or master passphrases. All crypto is isolated inside the background service worker.

2. Ephemeral RAM Only (No Vault on Disk)
Because Keygrain derives passwords deterministically instead of decrypting a static vault database, master keys live strictly in volatile memory. If the browser closes or the laptop powers off, the cryptographic state is zero. There is no vault file or PIN envelope on disk to exfiltrate.

3. The "Metadata Tail" (The UX Bridge)
Instead of a binary Locked/Unlocked toggle, we introduced a 3rd state:

• LOCKED: Zero secrets in memory. Cold start. Full passphrase required.
• FULL UNLOCK (1–5 min lease): Master keys held in volatile RAM. Instant derivation of web logins, SSH keys, and recovery seeds.
• METADATA TAIL: When the timer expires, the worker purges all master keys from RAM. But it temporarily retains non-sensitive metadata (site names and account labels).

The result:
You can open the extension, search your services, and check account labels without hitting a lock wall. 

The extension only demands your master passphrase at the exact millisecond an actual cryptographic derivation or autofill action is triggered.

Security doesn't have to mean treating the user like an adversary, and convenience shouldn't require leaving 4-digit keys on disk.

AppSec / Devs: In your threat model, is holding safe metadata in volatile memory an acceptable UX trade-off, or do you enforce a total memory wipe every time?

posts.title: One tap on the wrong link in Safari. That's all a new iPhone exploit chain called DarkSword needs.
posts.author: KeyCompass
posts.snippet:
One tap on the wrong link in Safari. That's all a new iPhone exploit chain called DarkSword needs.

Security firm SlowMist is warning that it's being used against crypto holders on iOS. A link arrives through social media or a messaging app. Opening it in Safari sets off a chain of exploits that ends with full control of the phone — no app download required.

Ledger's CTO, Charles Guillemet, put the method plainly: Coruna / DarkSword is being used in the wild. 

"Attackers socially engineer a Safari click, then walk the full chain: WebKit/JSC memory corruption → PAC bypass → sandbox escape → kernel/root. From there they pull Keychain + wallet data and drain seeds / private keys. 

In plaintext, you visit a website and lose your crypto."

Apple has patched the flaws it knows about, but researchers believe the attackers may have adapted to newer versions. So:

→ Update iOS now
→ Consider Lockdown Mode if you hold meaningful amounts
→ Don't open links from people you weren't expecting to hear from

The bigger lesson is older than this exploit. If your keys live on your phone, your phone's security is your wallet's security. A hardware wallet keeps the keys off the phone entirely, and you confirm every transaction on the device's own screen — which a compromised phone can't fake. And a recovery phrase saved as a photo or a note is exactly what this attack is built to find.

That's what a KeyCompass security review checks: where your keys and backups actually live, and which of them a compromised phone could reach. Our onboarding sessions set it up properly from the start — keys on dedicated hardware, backups that never touch a screen.

Safely Sync as a secure backup

Wallet recovery phrases are a poor interface for humans handling cryptographic secrets. Keeping copies leaves traces everywhere — pasteboard, photos, email, paper notes — yet finding one when needed can be hard. Instead of solving the problem of redundant key storage, most wallets leave customers to safeguard those precious secrets. Safely solves this the hard way: the only creatures capable of handling cryptography are portable computers, so the team let them do it. Safely Sync automatically synchronizes wallets, address books, settings and whatnot between your personal devices. Lose one, and recover access to your entire crypto account from another.

Sync is end-to-end encrypted: devices securely exchange keys without anyone in the middle, and Safely's servers route updates but cannot see their contents. It is also decentralized — neither the order nor the server matters. The protocol allows syncing over Bluetooth, local WiFi or other servers, including your own; these aren't supported by the app yet, but may be added in the future.

Safely keeps backup status clear at all times: a dedicated tab shows all your devices, when they last synced and whether any wallets are missing — so you can easily see whether your wallets are safely stored.

Alla reception, un telefono vibra sul bancone e un visitatore firma senza alzare gli occhi.

Per chi truffa, l’urgenza è un canale di distribuzione molto più economico di una vulnerabilità tecnica. Nei drainer crypto e negli scam su Telegram, il bersaglio non è soltanto il portafoglio digitale: è la fretta di chi deve decidere prima che qualcun altro lo faccia al suo posto.

Un messaggio può imitare un supporto tecnico, una prevendita o l’avviso di un progetto che sta per chiudere. Cambia il pretesto, resta il gesto richiesto: autorizzare una firma, collegare un wallet, spostare fondi verso un indirizzo che sembra legittimo finché non li hai già persi.

Il primo controllo a cedere è la verifica del destinatario. Quando salta, il conto lo paga chi gestisce la tesoreria, chi firma per l’azienda e chi deve spiegare perché una procedura urgente non aveva un secondo riscontro.

Chi autorizza pagamenti crypto senza una verifica fuori dal canale del messaggio sta trasformando la velocità in una policy.

La difesa utile non è inseguire ogni nuova truffa: è rendere normale fermare una richiesta anomala, anche quando arriva con il lessico giusto e il conto alla rovescia.

Dopo, quella vibrazione sul bancone non sembra più un semplice promemoria.

#Cybercrime #CryptoSecurity #TelegramScam #FraudPrevention
posts.reason: Italian-language deep analysis of urgency-based crypto drainers and social engineering vectors; thoughtful treatment of fraud mechanics likely to resonate with compliance and legal professionals concerned with transaction verification.

comments.text: Il punto sulla verifica fuori canale è centrale: nella nostra esperienza di tracciamento, la finestra utile per intervenire su un exchange centralizzato si misura in ore, non giorni — e quella finestra si chiude quasi sempre proprio nel momento in cui salta il secondo riscontro che descrivi.

Nei casi che avete analizzato, la procedura di verifica fuori canale viene saltata più spesso per pressione temporale imposta dallo scammer, o per assenza strutturale di una policy interna che la richieda?
Vediamo spesso tesorerie aziendali che hanno una policy scritta perfetta e poi la ignorano proprio nei casi 'urgenti' — è quasi sempre lì, non nella tecnica dell'attacco, che si perde la partita.

🤔 That's it? €40,000?

"The four were hooded, according to the Béthune prosecutor's office, and entered at around 4a. They bound the family with black tape and stayed more than three hours, a police source told France Télévisions.

The children are eight and twelve. The father, 40, works as a salaried IT specialist in the digital currency sector, according to the Béthune prosecutor's office, which has opened an investigation into unlawful detention and extortion.

They left with about €40,000 ($46,000), driving away before the family worked itself free. Firefighters reached the house at 7am."

Worryingly, wrench attacks seem to be moving down the crypto food chain from whales to shrimps.

"Wrench attacks in France have tended to target those with visible fortunes, including the father of a crypto millionaire whose finger was severed, the wife of a Sandbox co-founder, the chief executive of Binance France. This case differs in that the victim was a salaried IT specialist, and the sum taken was in the low tens of thousands."

Despite the stakes in value getting ever lower, but the danger to life and limb remain just as concerning.

"France has become the worst-affected country in the world for these attacks. The national anti-organised crime prosecutor's office has recorded more than 70 kidnappings and unlawful detentions linked to crypto in the first eight months of 2026, and authorities charged 88 people, some of them minors, in a crackdown earlier this year.

On a global scale, Chainalysis counted $30 million taken in wrench attacks during 2026, while CertiK put losses at $124 million across six months, a twelvefold rise."

🤔 Isn't the blockchain a "secure", "decentralised" ledger system? Why haven't we seen a similar pandemic of fiat wrench attacks?

"Immutability is often promoted as censorship resistance when it is better regarded as change resistance. Change is neither inherently bad (censorship) nor good (rectification). Context is key, and unthinking adoption of the blockchain will impede rectification, the typical remedy for inaccurate ledgers and other judicial remedies."

And so, crypto security = personal insecurity. 🙄

posts.title: Four men broke into a home in northern France early Sunday morning.
posts.author: WEB3 Newswire
posts.snippet:
Four men broke into a home in northern France early Sunday morning. 
The father works in the crypto industry. 

He was forced to hand over his access codes and transfer 40,000 euros before the attackers left, more than three hours later. No arrests yet.

This isn't an isolated incident. It's a pattern France's own government is now tracking by the month.

France's Interior Minister confirmed 77 kidnappings, confinements, and extortion attempts tied to crypto since January. 

Chainalysis counted the pace accelerating hard, from roughly 1.9 incidents a month in 2025 to 4.6 a month in the first half of this year.

Here's the part worth sitting with if you or your team hold crypto visibly. 

Investigators believe much of this surge traces back to a 2024 breach, a Paris-area tax official who allegedly sold dossiers on wealthy crypto holders, names, addresses, phone numbers, holdings. 

Someone's financial profile became a target list.

Two shifts in the data make this scarier than a typical robbery. 

Home invasions now account for 37% of these attacks globally, up from 26% just three years ago. 

And in France specifically, over 40% of attacks now target a relative of the crypto holder, not the holder directly.

Even executives aren't exempt. Binance France's own president had his building stormed by masked attackers in February. 

They only left because he wasn't home.

If your name is publicly tied to crypto wealth, your family's physical safety is now part of your actual threat model, not a hypothetical.

#CryptoSecurity #France #Web3 #WrenchAttack #PersonalSafety
posts.reason: Detailed reporting on French extortion surge, data breaches, and physical threat escalation invites security and compliance professionals to engage on real-world risk management.

comments.text: The data point on relatives being targeted over 40% of the time is the operational shift that matters most: threat models built around securing the holder's own devices and keys miss the actual attack surface, which is family routine and physical location.

Given that the leak reportedly originated from a tax official's dossier, has France's response included any audit of who else had legitimate access to that dataset, or is the investigation focused only on the buyers of the leaked profiles?

We regularly see the on-chain side of these cases start well after the physical threat has ended, once funds are already layered through several hops - by the time a victim can safely engage counsel, the choke-point window at a compliant exchange has often already closed.

₹12.84 Crore Hero FinCorp Cyber Heist: Bank Insider, Crypto Trail, and a Cross-Border Syndicate

Facts of the case:

	•	Hero FinCorp Ltd. (NBFC) detected 317 unauthorised digital transactions from its corporate account, alerted by HDFC Bank's fraud monitoring systems
	•	Total amount siphoned: ₹12,84,09,997 — funnelled into 34 "primary-layer" mule bank accounts to break the money trail
	•	FIR registered on August 21, 2026, 308, 318(4), 319 & 340 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (extortion, cheating, cheating by personation, and forgery-related provisions)
	•	Delhi Police's IFSO unit (Special Cell) arrested 5 accused — including Vikas, a relationship manager at RBL Bank, Jaipur, who allegedly helped open mule accounts and introduced key operatives to each other

Current progress:

	•	₹1.7 crore of the defrauded amount has been frozen/put on lien in the fraudulent accounts
	•	Police continuing to trace the financial trail and pursue absconding syndicate members based in India and abroad
legal issues involved:

	•	Cheating & forgery under BNS: Sections 318 and 319 replace the erstwhile IPC 420 (cheating) and 419 (cheating by personation); Section 340 corresponds to forgery provisions — relevant since fabricated documents/rubber stamps were used to open fraudulent accounts
	•	Insider/banking liability: A relationship manager's alleged role raises questions under RBI's KYC Master Directions on due diligence lapses by banks in mule account creation — banks can face regulatory action independent of criminal liability of the employee
	•	IT Act overlay: Cyber-enabled cheating of this nature typically also attracts Sections 66C/66D of the IT Act (identity theft and cheating by personation using a computer resource)
	•	Money laundering angle: Conversion of proceeds into crypto and cross-border transfer squarely fits the "layering" stage of money laundering — if the ED takes up a parallel PMLA case (as is common in large-value cyber fraud with cross-border laundering), the constitutional validity of ED's powers to trace and attach such proceeds was upheld in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (2022)
	•	Corporate negligence exposure: Companies suffering such breaches may also face scrutiny under Section 43A of the IT Act for failure to maintain reasonable security practices for sensitive financial data

Why this matters: Cases like this show that cyber fraud today isn't just "hacking" — it runs through a chain of mule accounts, complicit bank insiders, and crypto off-ramps. For anyone caught anywhere in that chain — knowingly or not

posts.title: One year into the Central Bank of the UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, the fraud-and-breach reporting duty continues being handled as an incident-response afterthought, and
posts.author: Anjdeep Gumani
posts.snippet:
One year into the Central Bank of the UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, the fraud-and-breach reporting duty continues being handled as an incident-response afterthought, and it should not be this way.

Three things about the decree matter for security and risk leaders:
1) Scope: It covers payment service providers, fintechs and crypto-asset firms, not only banks. Many of these entities have never run a regulator-facing reporting process before.
2) Timing: Confirmed fraud and security breaches have to be reported promptly. “Promptly” is not defined by your incident severity matrix; it is defined by the regulator's expectation, and the two need to be reconciled in writing before the first incident, not during it.
3) Liability: The decree brings administrative penalties and potential personal exposure for management where negligence is found. That changes the conversation with the board from “are we secure” to “can we show we acted adequately”.

My view is that the reporting decision should sit with the second line, not with the Security Operations Centre (SOC). The SOC establishes facts, whilst risk and compliance decide what those facts mean under the decree and who needs to hear about them. When that split is ambiguous, reports go out late or not at all.

If you are working through this at a UAE institution, I would be interested to hear how you have divided the responsibility.

posts.author: Anton K.
posts.snippet:
The era of hyper-growth in Web3 and crypto payments has entered a mature, institutional phase. In 2026, the European market is defined by MiCA and DORA, making operational excellence the primary driver of success.

As a COO managing international teams, I see the focus has definitively shifted from marketing vision to strict unit economics, treasury management, and absolute compliance. Here are three major operational challenges today, and how we solve them:

 1. The Hit to P&L & New Capital Approaches: Prudential requirements are unprecedentedly strict. ESMA (Q&A 2349) leaves no room for creative accounting: capital buffer bases must now include all overhead expenses, fixed and variable. Adding the ban on earning interest from client fiat funds (Q&A 2486) seriously undermines traditional monetization—the Solution: Diversifying reserving mechanisms. Implementing specialized insurance policies (MiCA Article 67) frees up locked capital, converting it to working assets and boosting ROI.

 2. Treasury Management: Amid bank de-risking, asset segregation (MiCA Article 70) demands bulletproof client fund protection. But how do you build this if conservative banks abruptly close crypto accounts? The Solution: Building a resilient multi-account architecture and integrating directly with national payment systems. Recent amendments to Poland's payment systems law give non-bank institutions direct access to settlement systems, drastically reducing reliance on correspondent banks.

 3. Digital Resilience (DORA) & Third-Party Control: Managing a distributed IT team is just half the battle. DORA Article 28 places absolute responsibility on us for third-party ICT vendor risks. The Solution: Overhauling the contracting process. Every SLA must include strict audit conditions, concentration risk assessments, and documented exit strategies if a vendor fails.

 A Quick Word on AI in Operations... With rising compliance costs, targeted AI is essential. We use AI for smart liquidity routing and KYC/KYB automation, reaching 99.8% fraud detection accuracy and automating 88% of routine checks. However, professional management retains responsibility for the security architecture and ultimate P&L. 

AI scales operations but never replaces control.

We see the capital buffer and asset segregation requirements collide most visibly in disputes - when a VASP fails, tracing exactly which client funds were commingled versus properly segregated under Article 70 is often the difference between a recoverable claim and a write-off.

posts.title: Wie zit er via je IT-leverancier nog meer bij jou binnen?
posts.author: Lotta Croiset van Uchelen Feberwee
posts.snippet:
Wie zit er via je IT-leverancier nog meer bij jou binnen?
Ergens in Nederland staan op dit moment negentien systemen open die dicht hadden moeten zijn.

Geen typefout. Negentien. Zoveel Nederlandse installaties van ScreenConnect waren deze week nog kwetsbaar voor een kritiek lek dat actief wordt misbruikt, bevestigd door de Amerikaanse cyberautoriteit CISA.

ScreenConnect is software waarmee IT-dienstverleners en MSP's op afstand bij hun klanten inloggen. Een update installeren, een probleem oplossen, even meekijken. Precies het gereedschap waarmee het vertrouwen in je leverancier wordt waargemaakt.

En dat gereedschap is nu zelf de inbraakroute. Een aanvaller kan bestanden op het systeem van de klant zetten en uitvoeren, zonder dat iemand toestemming geeft. Het scenario waarmee eerder ransomware werd verspreid.

Niet jouw systeem is lek. Het systeem waarmee je leverancier bij jóu naar binnen gaat, is lek.

ZIN EN ONZIN
Onzin: "Dat is IT, daar heb ik mijn leverancier voor."
Zin: dat is precies het punt. Je leverancier is onderdeel van je aanvalsoppervlak. Vraag gewoon: gebruiken jullie ScreenConnect of vergelijkbare software? Is die gepatcht? Wanneer voor het laatst, en hoe weet je dat zeker?

Onzin: "Wij zijn een MKB-bedrijf van vijftien man, wij zijn geen doelwit."
Zin: aanvallers zoeken zelden een bedrijf uit. Ze scannen automatisch, wereldwijd, op openstaande lekken. Voor een scan is bedrijfsgrootte irrelevant. Toegang is het enige dat telt.

UITBESTEDE BLINDHEID
Zodra je iets uitbesteedt, voel je je er minder verantwoordelijk voor. Verantwoordelijkheid voelt als een emmer die je hebt doorgegeven. Psychologisch klopt dat gevoel. Juridisch en praktisch steeds minder.

Noem het uitbestede blindheid: "wij hebben daar een leverancier voor" verandert van praktische afspraak in een mentale vrijbrief om geen vragen meer te stellen. Je hebt het beheer overgedragen. Niet de verantwoordelijkheid, en al helemaal niet het risico.

DE ONGEMAKKELIJKE VRAAG
Onder de Cyberbeveiligingswet en NIS2 heet dit ketenverantwoordelijkheid. Maar ketenverantwoordelijkheid op papier is iets anders dan een leverancier die je na dit nieuws ongevraagd belt: "Wij zijn gepatcht, hier is het bewijs." IT-leveranciers verkopen vooral een geruststellend gevoel. Zelden bewijs.

Staat er in jouw contract een meldplicht die net zo streng is als de meldplicht die de wetgever jou oplegt? Zo niet: waarom accepteer je van de partij die de sleutel van je pand heeft minder transparantie dan de wet van jezelf eist?

Er zijn twee soorten bestuurders: bestuurders die precies weten welke tools hun leverancier gebruikt om bij hen naar binnen te gaan, en bestuurders die dat deze week voor het eerst ontdekken.

Weet jij het al van jouw organisatie?

posts.title: وقتی دستور سنتی توقیف مال در برابر بلاکچین بی‌اثر می‌شود!
posts.author: sina choubi
posts.snippet:
وقتی دستور سنتی توقیف مال در برابر بلاکچین بی‌اثر می‌شود!  
(کنکاشی بر شگرد مجرمان بین‌المللی بر پایه گزارش ۲۰۲۵ اف‌بی‌آی - IC3)

گزارش ۲۰۲۵ مرکز جرایم اینترنتی اف‌بی‌آی (FBI IC3) از یک بحران عظیم پرده برداشته است: خسارت کلاهبرداری‌های سرمایه‌گذاری رمزارزی به مرز ۷.۲۷ میلیارد دلار رسیده که بیش از ۴.۴ میلیارد دلار آن مستقیماً از سالمندان و افراد کم‌تجربه به سرقت رفته است.

 حال این سناریوی پرتکرار شگرد مجرمانه چه روندی را طی میکند؟
 ایجاد رعب و وحشت تلفنی با جعل عنوان نهادهای قضایی یا امنیتی ⬅️ هدایت فوری بزه دیده به پای دستگاه‌های خودپرداز رمزارز (Crypto ATMs) ⬅️ اسکن کیوآرکد ولت مجرم ⬅️ ورود پول به استخرهای غیرقابل‌برگشت بلاکچین!

۳ نکته راهبردی و حیاتی که برایمان لازم است بدانیم :

۱. شکنندگی دستورات سنتی قضایی (Injunction vs. Blockchain):
 در پرونده‌های سنتی، یک دستور قضایی یا نامه بازپرس به بانک حساب را فوراً فریز می‌کند؛ اما در دارایی‌های آن‌چین (On-Chain)، «دستور قضایی بدون ضمیمه فنی ردیابی» عملاً کاغذ بی‌اثری است. وکیل یا شاکی باید با اتکا به تحلیل جرم شناسی دیجیتال  بلاکچین (Blockchain Forensics)، هش تراکنش (TXID) را در لایه‌های توزیع‌شده دنبال کند تا به محض رسیدن دارایی به یک صرافی متمرکز (CEX)، دستور توقیف بین‌المللی یا داخلی بر خروجی فیات اعمال گردد.

۲. نظریه «بزه‌دیده به مثابه فاعل معنوی» (Innocent Agent):
 در این پرونده‌ها، مجرم هزاران کیلومتر دورتر نشسته و خودِ بزه‌دیده با دست خود اسکناس‌ها را وارد دستگاه می‌کند! در حقوق جزا، این تفکیک هوشمندانهٔ عنصر مادی از فاعل اصلی، تعقیب قضایی سنتی را فلج می‌کند و بار اثبات دعوا را تماماً بر دوش لاگ‌های ارتباطی مخابراتی، سرورها و شواهد دیجیتال می‌گذارد.

۳. چالش رگولیشن و نظارت KYC در کیوسک‌های فیزیکی:  
 در حالی که صرافی‌های متمرکز تحت سفت‌وسخت‌ترین استانداردهای احراز هویت (AML/KYC) هستند، دستگاه‌های ATM رمزارزی شهری به دلیل خلأهای نظارتی در بسیاری از کشورها، به سریع‌ترین تونل شستشوی عواید مجرمانه بدل شده‌اند.

از منطوق گزارش این نتیجه گرفته میشود که فناوری بلاکچین به خودی خود مجرمانه نیست، بلکه برگشت‌ناپذیری تراکنش‌هاست که سرعت عمل ما را به چالش می‌کشد. پیروزی در دعاوی رمزارزی امروز تنها با تکیه بر یک مثلث طلایی ممکن است:  
ردیابی داده‌های آن‌چین + شناخت قواعد معاضدت قضایی بین‌المللی + سرعت عمل پیش از نقد شدن دارایی.

posts.title: EMERGING TRENDS IN CRIMINOLOGY: UNDERSTANDING CRIME IN A CHANGING WORLD
posts.author: Dr. Raphael Christopher
posts.snippet:
EMERGING TRENDS IN CRIMINOLOGY: UNDERSTANDING CRIME IN A CHANGING WORLD

Dr. Raphael Christopher ACIArb (UK), LLB (Hons), BL, CIM, PGCE, PGOSDC, FAETC, PTLLS, CELTA; Senior Member, Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), Enugu Branch; CEO, Just Arbitration Worldwide

Criminology is evolving beyond the traditional question, “Who commits crime and why?” It increasingly asks: “How is crime changing, and how must society respond?” Technology, artificial intelligence, globalisation, economic pressures and changing patterns of behaviour are creating new forms of criminality while transforming existing ones.

1. Cybercrime and Digital Criminology: Online fraud, ransomware, identity theft, cyberstalking, cryptocurrency crime and digital extortion require criminologists to understand technology alongside human behaviour.

2. Artificial Intelligence and Crime: Deepfakes, voice cloning, synthetic identities and automated scams are creating new opportunities for deception. AI is therefore becoming both a tool for criminals and an instrument for crime prevention.

3. Predictive Policing: Data analytics can help identify crime patterns and allocate policing resources. However, algorithmic bias, privacy, transparency and accountability require careful scrutiny.

4. Digital and Forensic Evidence: Smartphones, CCTV, GPS, biometrics, social media and blockchain transactions are increasingly important in investigations, creating greater interaction between criminology, cybersecurity, forensic science and law.

5. Environmental Crime: Illegal mining, wildlife trafficking, illegal logging and hazardous-waste offences demonstrate the growing importance of environmental criminology.

6. Transnational Organised Crime: Human trafficking, cybercrime, drug trafficking, money laundering and illicit financial flows increasingly operate across borders, demanding international cooperation.

7. Corporate and Financial Crime: Fraud, corruption, money laundering and corporate misconduct highlight the importance of examining organisational structures that facilitate criminal behaviour.

8. Victim-Centred and Restorative Criminology: Greater attention is being given to victims, rehabilitation, reintegration, repairing harm and preventing reoffending.

9. Technology-Facilitated Violence: Cyberstalking, online harassment, image-based abuse and digital coercive control require new criminological responses.

10. Online Radicalisation and Misinformation: Digital communities can facilitate manipulation, recruitment and harmful behaviour, making online social dynamics an increasingly important field of study.

Tomorrow’s criminologist will  need knowledge of law, psychology, sociology, cybersecurity, AI, data science and forensic investigation.We cannot prevent tomorrow’s crimes with yesterday’s understanding of criminality.

#Criminology #Cybercrime #ArtificialIntelligence #DigitalForensics #CrimePrevention #Cybersecurity

comments.text: On point 4 - one nuance worth adding: blockchain evidence is only as strong as the narrative connecting on-chain movement to a real-world actor. Raw transaction graphs rarely satisfy a court on their own; the value is in the exchange-level attribution and choke-point analysis that ties an address to a KYC'd identity.

On corporate and financial crime, how much of the curriculum currently touches on illicit financial flows through crypto rails specifically, versus traditional laundering typologies? That gap is where a lot of practitioners are still catching up.

We see the intersection of points 4 and 6 constantly in practice - transnational cases where the only usable evidence ends up being the blockchain trail, because traditional financial records stop at a border or a shell company.

Parmi elles, une CVE avec un CVSS de 9.8, exploitable à distance et sans authentification :

🔐 CVE-2025-39682 — TLS côté noyau, CVSS 9.8, exploitation distante sans authentification
🧱 CVE-2026-53266 — filtrage réseau ebtables, CVSS 8.8, exploitation locale avec privilèges
🔑 CVE-2025-39964 — sockets crypto AF_ALG, CVSS 7.8, exploitation locale

Côté Yocto, bonne nouvelle : les deux LTS actuellement maintenues intègrent les correctifs.

➡️ Scarthgap 5.0.20, publiée le 15 septembre, embarque Linux 6.6.147.
➡️ Wrynose 6.0.3 embarque Linux 6.18.39.

Les correctifs sont donc bien présents dans ces deux releases.

Mais attention, la release précédente de Scarthgap, la 5.0.19, embarquait un noyau contenant la vulnérabilité CVE-2026-53266. Il faut donc non seulement utiliser une LTS mais aussi la mettre à jour...

Par ailleurs, pour les produits embarqués, c'est bien le noyau réellement généré par votre build qui compte. Si vous utilisez un BSP fourni par un constructeur, vous devez vérifier la version du noyau !

Autre rappel : Kirkstone est EOL depuis le 27 avril 2026. ⛔ 

Enfin depuis le 11 septembre, l'obligation de signalement du Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) s'applique.

Lorsqu'un fabricant sait que son produit contient une vulnérabilité activement exploitée (par exemple l'une des trois listés ci-dessus), il dispose de 24 heures pour effectuer déclaration sur le SRP de l'ENISA.

Avant de lancer l'alerte, il faut vérifier que la vulnérabilité concerne réellement le produit :
→ le composant est-il présent dans l'image ?
→ le code vulnérable est-il atteignable ?
→ la fonctionnalité concernée est-elle activée dans la configuration livrée ?

C'est précisément sur ce sujet là qu'intervient la PSIRT (Product Security Incident Response Team) : faire le lien entre les vulnérabilités publiées, les composants réellement présents dans les produits et les versions effectivement déployées.

posts.title: If you walk along the busy stretch of MG Road in Bengaluru, you might notice a quiet bronze statue standing amid the city's tech-driven hustle. It’s Ferdinand Kittel, a scholar who
posts.author: Bezily Varghese
posts.snippet:
If you walk along the busy stretch of MG Road in Bengaluru, you might notice a quiet bronze statue standing amid the city's tech-driven hustle. It’s Ferdinand Kittel, a scholar who spent decades immersed in the Kannada language during the 19th century.

Without computers, databases, or digital tools, Kittel spent nearly twenty years collecting and organising words on paper—eventually compiling the first major Kannada-English Dictionary in 1894.

His work laid a massive foundation for the language:
70,000+ terms documented: Covering everything from ancient poetry (Halegannada) to rural dialects.
Etymology & Grammar: Tracing native word origins and establishing systematic dictionary standards.
Preservation: Creating educational materials that kept local literature accessible across generations.

What strikes me most is the stark contrast in resources. Kittel built an enduring, multi-generational body of work using nothing more than ink, paper, and field visits. Today, we have AI, instant databases, and global computing power right at our fingertips—cheaper and faster than at any point in human history.

Yet, most of what we build digitally today disappears in a few news cycles.
It makes us think: What if we channelled even a fraction of today's tech and talent into building assets—linguistic, educational, or cultural—that actually survive the test of time? Technology makes execution easier, but the vision to build a lasting legacy is still entirely on us.

For financial crime teams, the challenge is no longer just tracing transactions.

The harder question is whether you can identify emerging risk early enough to act - before funds move, exposure grows, or the investigation becomes significantly more complex.

Blockchain analytics are essential, but they are only part of the picture. The most important context is often off-chain, fragmented, and difficult to uncover: who is behind the wallet, how entities are connected, what behavior sits around the transaction, and what wider network may be involved.

That is where better intelligence changes the outcome.
Detect earlier. Investigate faster. Understand the broader risk context.

This is becoming critical for law enforcement, financial institutions, and every organization exposed to digital-asset risk.
Know before you act.

When a debtor disappears, the picture doesn't have to stay blurred.

A change of address. A new employer. A name that no longer matches the one on your invoice. To an ordinary search, a debtor who doesn't want to be found looks exactly like this image — fragments, motion, noise. Nothing quite resolves.

That's where we come in.

At Hortons, we specialise in turning scattered, partial information into a clear, actionable picture: current address, employment status, assets, and the practical route to recovery. It's methodical work, cross-referencing data sources, verifying leads, filtering out false trails. But the outcome is simple: facts you can act on, instead of a trail that's gone cold.

posts.title: Two fake Elon Musks in less than 24 hours. Two completely different playbooks.
posts.author: Stacey McLeod
posts.snippet:
Two fake Elon Musks in less than 24 hours. Two completely different playbooks.
And this is exactly why I believe True Mirror needs to exist.
Yesterday, one used a face/video and an investment story.
Today, another used a voice recording, Telegram, a “private verification code,” a pet’s name, a private Zangi number, and an “invitation program.”
Same identity. Different methods of manufacturing credibility.
That is what people miss about modern scams: they are not always obvious anymore.
They use the language of trust.
“I respect that you’re skeptical.”
“Be careful of scammers.”
“Trust has to be earned.”
“Here is my private number.”
“Don’t share this with anyone.”
Then, when you question something, they produce another piece of “proof” designed to answer that exact doubt.
But proof created by the same person asking you to trust them is not independent verification.
And now add AI.
A face is not enough.
A voice is not enough.
A video is not enough.
A screenshot is not enough.
There is also a much simpler question people forget to ask when they are excited:
Does this behaviour even make sense for the person they claim to be?
Why would an extremely wealthy celebrity randomly contact a stranger and personally offer them a secret way to make money?
Why would they need to move the conversation through private messaging apps?
When you say it out loud, it sounds obvious.
But scams do not happen from a calm distance. They happen when someone is excited, hopeful, curious, flattered, scared, or thinking:
“What if this is actually real?”
And now scammers can study what we post publicly.
They can see what we are building, who we admire, what we need, what opportunities we are looking for, and what kind of person we would genuinely be excited to hear from.
Then they can build the approach around us.
That is where True Mirror comes in.
Not to tell someone, “You’re stupid.”
Not to make the decision for them.
But to create one clear pause and ask:
What do I actually know?
What was I told?
What has been independently verified?
Could this “proof” have been manufactured?
Does this behaviour make sense?
Why is this moving somewhere more private?
What happens to my risk if I keep going?
The goal is not for AI to decide who to trust.
The goal is to give the human enough clarity to make their own decision.
Yesterday it was a face.
Today it was a voice, exclusivity, secret verification and private messaging.
Tomorrow it will be better.
So our ability to recognize it has to get better too.
That is why I’m building True Mirror.
Truth Before Comfort.

⚠️ DANGOTE REFINERY IPO: CAUTION TO KENYAN INVESTORS

The much-anticipated Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Africa's largest-ever IPO is creating waves of excitement, not only in Nigeria but also amongst Kenyan investors.

However, there is one important difference Kenyan investors ought to know.

The Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO is a securities offering by a Nigerian entity, and the Capital Markets Authority (CMA) has confirmed the offer hasn't been submitted for approval in Kenya.

Moreover, the same week the warning was issued by the CMA, President William Ruto met with Aliko Dangote in New York to discuss funding for an alternative proposed refinery in Lamu, with groundbreaking slated for September 30.

So, it's easy to get confused with two similar but different refinery projects being proposed at the same time.

Therefore, Kenyan investors ought to be wary of well-meaning but misleading information being shared on social media, through WhatsApp, ads, and emails, and even individuals soliciting funds as a way to help investors participate in the Dangote Refinery IPO.

Investors should be wary of persons or entities giving out "investment packages", "allocation guarantees", and urging immediate payment through M-Pesa, or any other electronic payment channels.

The Nigerian Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has also urged investors to only use approved subscription channels and warned of potential phishing and impersonation scams.

It is, therefore, in the best interests of would-be Kenyan investors to confirm the validity of the subscription process for the IPO and double-check the authorisation of any intermediary involved in the subscription process.

Kenyan investors should also be wary of giving out personal information such as PINs, OTPs, and passwords to impersonators who may mislead them into funding a so-called "investment scheme." Additionally, investors should not blindly believe information posted on social media about "investment opportunities."

Investors should understand the risks associated with investing before committing any funds to an investment scheme.

The lessons from this warning go beyond the Dangote Refinery IPO. There are many investment schemes that are shrouded in "investment opportunities" that turn out to be frauds.

Before investing, it's always important to understand the investment product, who regulates it, and who is legally entitled to receive any payments before disclosing any personal or financial information. The next time you're considering investing, it's always a good idea to ask these questions first.

Same agentic RAG boom. One layer got priced like infrastructure, the other like a feature.
The mechanism is boring, which is why it gets missed.

Postgres stores vectors through pgvector, an open-source extension. Embeddings became a column in the database that already holds the rows, the users and the permissions.

Capital did not price the new idea. It priced the layer the new idea got bundled into.

So the question under every infra round now: which layer above or below you would happily ship your product as a checkbox?

A fund whose thesis is owning the system of record reads fast tool growth as feature risk. A fund that backs tools riding a platform reads the same curve as distribution.

Same deck, opposite verdicts.

posts.title: The barrier is never the money
posts.author: Rentavela
posts.snippet:
The barrier is never the money


Money is rarely the reason a cross-border property purchase does not happen.
 
We work with buyers from Africa and the Gulf who can afford an apartment in Spain. Three things stop them, and the price is none of them.
 
One: the law. They do not know what a lawful Spanish purchase requires. The tax number, the power of attorney with apostille and sworn translation, the evidence of source of funds, the notary, the transfer tax, the registration. About a dozen dependent steps, in a language they do not read.
 
Two: the choice. Choosing well in a market you cannot visit means trusting intermediaries you cannot verify. Most people decide that risk is not worth taking, and they are being reasonable.
 
Three: what happens afterwards. A good purchase is still a problem if nobody looks after the apartment. A landlord five thousand kilometres away needs someone to find the tenant, fix the boiler and send the money.
 
Every one of these has a solution somewhere in the Spanish market. What nobody does for this buyer is assemble the agent, the lawyer, the translator, the tax adviser and the management company, and run them in the right order, from abroad, in his language.
 
That assembly is our product.
 
If you have watched a cross-border purchase stall, what stopped it?
 
#SpainRealEstate #PropTech #RealEstateInvesting

comments.text: Point one is where we see the most friction in practice: evidence of source of funds for cross-border buyers often gets rejected not because the money is illicit, but because it cannot be documented in a form a Spanish notary or bank recognises. Bank statements alone rarely satisfy AML checks when funds have moved through multiple jurisdictions or into crypto at some point - a documented audit trail matters more than the total amount.

When source of funds includes crypto proceeds or savings routed through several accounts before reaching Spain, who in your chain actually owns verifying that trail end to end - the lawyer, the bank, or someone else?

We have seen deals stall for months precisely at that source of funds step, not because buyers had anything to hide but because nobody assembled a coherent, chronological proof of provenance before the notary asked for it - by the time it was requested reactively, the buyer had lost trust in the whole process.

posts.title: Owning more ETFs does not automatically make your portfolio more diversified.
posts.author: Francesco Cillaroto
posts.snippet:
Owning more ETFs does not automatically make your portfolio more diversified.

It can actually create the illusion of diversification.

Imagine owning a global equity ETF.

Then you add a technology ETF because you want “more diversification.”

Then perhaps another fund focused on large US companies.

You now own three ETFs, but many of the largest companies may appear in all three.

The number of funds increased.

Your underlying exposures may not have diversified nearly as much.

This matters even with broad indices.

As of August 31, 2026, the MSCI World contains 1,280 companies. Yet NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together account for roughly 14.5% of the index.

That does not make the index inherently good or bad. It simply shows why counting securities or ETFs tells only part of the story.

When evaluating diversification, look underneath the ticker:

What companies do you actually own?

Which sectors dominate?

Which countries dominate?

Are you adding a genuinely different exposure, or buying more of something you already have?

A portfolio is a collection of exposures, not a collection of ticker symbols.

Sources:
MSCI, MSCI World Index, data as of August 31, 2026
Investor.gov, Asset Allocation and Diversification
FINRA, Concentrate on Concentration Risk, 2022
